children.text: The Equity Gap That Value-Based Care Must Confront

Value-based care was designed to improve quality while reducing costs — a goal that sounds universal but has been implemented in ways that systematically exclude or disadvantage the people who most need better care. The promise of VBC is that if we pay for outcomes rather than volume, the entire health system will orient toward keeping people healthy and intervening effectively when they get sick. But that promise breaks down when the populations most likely to get sick are also the populations whose providers are most financially penalized for serving them, and whose social circumstances make achieving measured outcomes hardest.

Health disparities in the United States are pervasive, well-documented, and stubbornly persistent. Black Americans have shorter life expectancies than white Americans, higher rates of preventable hospitalizations, worse outcomes for nearly every major chronic disease, and less access to high-quality specialty care. Hispanic Americans face systematic barriers to accessing care due to language, immigration status, and geographic concentration in underserved communities. Rural Americans — regardless of race — face provider shortages, longer travel distances to specialists, and hospital closures that have accelerated over the past decade. These are not statistical abstractions; they are the lived experiences of tens of millions of Americans who depend on a healthcare system that was not designed with them in mind.

An analysis of U.S. county data (Hood et al., American Journal of Preventive Medicine, 2016) estimated that socioeconomic factors — income, education, employment, family and social support, community safety — account for about 47 percent of modifiable health outcomes, health behaviors for 34 percent, and clinical care for only 16 percent. This means that value-based programs focused exclusively on clinical quality metrics are, at best, optimizing a minority of the drivers of health. A VBC system that ignores social determinants is like a building code that focuses only on the foundation while ignoring whether the occupants have heat, water, and a safe neighborhood.

Social determinants of health — income, housing, education, food security, transportation, and neighborhood safety — together with health behaviors, account for roughly 80% of modifiable health outcomes, while clinical care accounts for about 16% (Hood et al., 2016). A value-based care system that ignores these upstream factors cannot achieve equitable health improvement, regardless of how well it optimizes clinical delivery.

children.text: How Current VBC Design Can Worsen Disparities

The architecture of most value-based payment programs contains features that can actively worsen health disparities, even when the programs' intentions are positive. The clearest example is financial benchmarking based on historical costs. When ACOs or hospitals have their savings targets set relative to their own historical spending, providers who historically underserved low-income populations — spending less not because of efficiency but because patients couldn't afford care — will have lower baselines and therefore must improve more to earn bonuses. Conversely, providers who historically overspent may generate "savings" simply by stopping unnecessary high-cost care, even without improving outcomes.

Quality metrics in VBC programs are similarly biased by the populations they measure. Preventive care rates, disease management outcomes, and patient experience scores are all sensitive to social determinants that providers cannot control. A physician practicing in a food desert who consistently struggles to improve her patients' HbA1c levels despite excellent clinical care faces the same performance benchmark as a physician in an affluent community where patients can afford fresh food, have stable employment, and can take time off to manage their chronic conditions. Without social risk adjustment, the quality measurement system punishes the former and rewards the latter.

Provider network and geographic access issues compound these problems. VBC programs are most effective when patients have consistent, ongoing relationships with their primary care providers — the foundation of care coordination and preventive care. But underserved communities have higher rates of safety-net provider dependence, federally qualified health center (FQHC) utilization, and emergency department use as primary care. These non-standard care patterns make attribution difficult in ACO models and reduce the effectiveness of care coordination interventions designed around assumptions of regular primary care visits.

body.message: Value-based care programs that penalize providers for serving disadvantaged populations create incentives for "cream skimming" — the strategic avoidance of high-risk, high-complexity, socially disadvantaged patients in favor of healthier, wealthier ones. When financial models reward efficiency over equity, providers who serve the most vulnerable patients can face the steepest penalties, creating pressure to deprioritize or exclude these populations from VBC arrangements.
body.title: The "Cream Skimming" Risk

children.text: The Social Determinants Framework in Practice

Addressing social determinants within a VBC framework requires moving beyond clinical-only interventions. Several models have demonstrated that systematic SDOH screening and community-based intervention — when integrated with clinical care delivery — can improve both health outcomes and financial performance. The logic is compelling: a patient who loses her apartment will generate emergency department visits, hospitalizations, and uncontrolled chronic disease management costs that dwarf the cost of housing support. If the VBC arrangement captures the savings from those avoided costs, investing in housing support can be financially rational, not just compassionate.

The Camden Coalition of Healthcare Providers in Camden, New Jersey pioneered the concept of "hotspotting" — identifying the highest-cost, most frequently hospitalized patients and providing intensive community-based support to address both clinical and social needs. Its wraparound services included housing assistance, transportation, medication management, and care coordination. When the approach was tested rigorously, however, the result was sobering: a randomized trial of the Coalition's care-transitions program (Finkelstein et al., New England Journal of Medicine, 2020) found 180-day readmission rates of 62.3 percent among enrolled patients versus 61.7 percent under usual care — no significant difference. The model still shaped complex care management nationally, and the trial is a standing lesson that promising before-and-after results need controlled evaluation.

The Vermont Blueprint for Health, whose multi-payer community health teams began in pilot communities in 2008, integrates community health teams — social workers, care coordinators, community health workers — with primary care practices. These teams address social needs alongside clinical needs. A peer-reviewed analysis of six years of Vermont all-payer claims (Jones et al., Population Health Management, 2016) associated the Blueprint's community-oriented medical-home model with lower expenditures and utilization while maintaining quality — one of the longest-running statewide examples of linking community supports to primary care.

body.content:
The Accountable Health Communities (AHC) Model, launched by CMMI in 2017, tested whether systematically identifying and addressing health-related social needs — through screening, referral, and community navigation — could reduce Medicare and Medicaid utilization and costs.
Twenty-eight bridge organizations screened more than 1 million Medicaid and Medicare beneficiaries for five core needs: housing instability, food insecurity, transportation problems, utility difficulties, and interpersonal violence. In the Assistance Track, navigation-eligible beneficiaries (at least one need plus two or more ED visits in the prior year) were randomized to referral information alone or referral plus an offer of navigation; the Alignment Track was not randomized. CMS's final evaluation found that navigation lowered total health care expenditures — with fewer inpatient admissions and readmissions among Medicaid beneficiaries and fewer ED visits and ambulatory-care-sensitive admissions among fee-for-service Medicare beneficiaries — even though rates of need resolution were similar to the control group.
body.title: CMS Accountable Health Communities Model

children.text: What an Equity-Centered VBC System Looks Like

Building a VBC system that works for everyone requires changes at multiple levels: the data infrastructure for measuring equity, the payment architecture that removes penalties for serving disadvantaged populations, the workforce that can address social and clinical needs together, and the community partnerships that connect healthcare systems to social services. None of these changes is simple, and all of them require sustained policy commitment across multiple administrations.

On measurement, equity-centered VBC requires stratifying all quality measures by race, ethnicity, income, disability status, and social risk factor status — and holding providers accountable for reducing within-panel disparities, not just improving average performance. CMS moved in this direction in 2023, finalizing a Health Equity Index reward for Medicare Advantage Star Ratings and a health equity adjustment for the Hospital Value-Based Purchasing program, but reversed both in 2025: the FY2026 inpatient rule removed the hospital adjustment, and the CY2027 Medicare Advantage rule did not implement the reward. But the data infrastructure for consistent race and ethnicity reporting in healthcare claims remains incomplete, and many providers cannot accurately stratify their own quality data by social characteristics.

On workforce, community health workers (CHWs) have emerged as one of the highest-value tools for bridging clinical care and social needs. CHWs are trusted community members who provide health education, navigation, care coordination, and social support — often in patients' homes and in community settings rather than clinical offices. In the CY2024 Physician Fee Schedule, CMS created Medicare's first Community Health Integration codes (G0019, G0022) for CHW services furnished under a billing practitioner's supervision; Medicaid coverage of CHW services remains a state option; in KFF's 2022 survey, 29 of 48 responding states reported allowing Medicaid payment for CHW services. This represents a significant structural change that could enable systematic SDOH intervention at scale.

children.text: The Policy Landscape and What Remains Unresolved

CMS has articulated a health equity commitment across multiple programs and policy documents, but translating that commitment into payment design that meaningfully advances equity is a work in progress. The Innovation Center's October 2021 Strategy Refresh named health equity a strategic objective, committing to embed it in every model. The AHC model, the Making Care Primary model, and ACO REACH all included equity-specific requirements or payment adjustments. Yet in March 2025 CMMI announced the early termination of four models — Making Care Primary among them — raising uncertainty about the long-term trajectory of equity-focused innovation.

Medicaid is potentially a more powerful lever for health equity in VBC than Medicare, because Medicaid disproportionately serves the populations with the most pronounced health disparities — low-income adults, children, people with disabilities, and pregnant women. Several states have moved aggressively to incorporate SDOH into Medicaid managed care contracts: North Carolina's Healthy Opportunities Pilots — described by the state as the nation's first comprehensive program to test evidence-based non-medical interventions for high-needs Medicaid enrollees — tested whether braiding healthcare and social service funding could improve outcomes for the most complex enrollees; services stopped on July 1, 2025, when state funding lapsed. Massachusetts, Oregon, and California have implemented similar Medicaid innovations.

The fundamental unresolved tension is between universalism and targeting. A truly equitable VBC system would require different standards, different investments, and different timelines for providers and populations at different starting points — a form of affirmative payment design that explicitly prioritizes closing gaps rather than maximizing average performance. American health policy has historically struggled with this kind of targeted approach, preferring universal standards that appear fair on paper but embed structural inequities in practice. Resolving that tension — acknowledging that equity sometimes requires differential treatment — is the defining political and policy challenge for the next generation of value-based care design.

body.analogy: A school system that grades every student on the same curve regardless of whether they had tutors, stable housing, and enough food is not measuring academic achievement — it is measuring socioeconomic advantage. Value-based care faces the same problem: measuring health outcomes on a single universal scale when the determinants of those outcomes are profoundly unequal.
body.concept: Health Equity and VBC Performance Measurement

points: Social determinants of health — income, housing, education, food security, and transportation — together with health behaviors, drive roughly 80 percent of modifiable health outcomes, meaning VBC programs focused only on clinical quality metrics are optimizing a minority of what actually drives health.

Current VBC program design can worsen disparities through historical cost benchmarking, unadjusted quality metrics, and financial penalties that disproportionately fall on safety-net providers serving the most disadvantaged populations.

The "cream skimming" risk — providers strategically avoiding high-complexity, socially disadvantaged patients — is a real consequence of VBC financial models that penalize rather than reward serving vulnerable populations.

Community health workers, SDOH screening programs, and cross-sector partnerships between healthcare and social services represent promising operational strategies for addressing social determinants within VBC arrangements.

The Vermont Blueprint for Health and CMS Accountable Health Communities Model provide real-world evidence that linking community supports to primary care, and social-needs screening to navigation, can lower spending and hospital-based use.

CMS made health equity a design objective for Innovation Center models in 2021 and created Medicare billing codes for community health integration and SDOH risk assessment in 2024 — but in 2025 it rolled back several equity provisions, so equity-adjusted payment design remains unsettled.

Building a VBC system that works for everyone requires stratified quality measurement, social risk adjustment, universal SDOH screening, community health integration, and outcome accountability for demonstrated disparity reduction — not just average performance improvement.

body.explanation: The AHC Model specifically tested the clinical and financial impact of screening beneficiaries for five health-related social needs — housing instability, food insecurity, transportation, utilities, and interpersonal safety — and then providing community navigation to connect them with social services. CMS's final evaluation found that navigation lowered total health care expenditures and hospital-based use among navigation-eligible beneficiaries (fewer inpatient admissions for Medicaid enrollees, fewer ED visits for fee-for-service Medicare enrollees), supporting the premise that addressing social needs can reduce utilization and cost.
